### checks — `checks/`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpaceAxiomChecks` | Mixin that gives any HilbertSpace subclass a randomized self-test of the Hilbert space axioms via a single public method `.check()`. | `pygeoinf2.testing.check_space / check_coordinates (free functions)` | The mixin is gone from the HilbertSpace MRO (no .check() on any v2 space: grep 'def check(' over pygeoinf2 minus tests finds nothing). Its content is split into two free functions: check_space(space, *, rng, trials=5, rebuild) for the metric-free axioms and check_coordinates(space, *, rng, trials=5) for everything that touches to_components/from_components/basis_vector, which now only runs on a CoordinateSpace (it raises AssertionError otherwise, testing.py:240-244). No progress printing; a seedable numpy Generator replaces the global RNG; comparisons are made in the space norm rather than on component arrays. The GaussianMeasure sampling option has no counterpart. The copy-independence and in-place-mutation checks are weaker than v1's (see their rows). |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpaceAxiomChecks.check` | Runs the once-only checks (Gram-Schmidt, basis vectors + sample_expectation) and then `n_checks` randomized trials of the vector-space, inner-product, mapping round-trip, in-place (ax/axpy) and copy checks, each trial drawing fresh x, y, z samples and scalars a, b ~ randn(). | `testing.check_space(space, /, *, rng=None, trials=5, rebuild=None) -> None` | space.check(n_checks=10, measure=None) becomes check_space(space, rng=, trials=, rebuild=). n_checks -> trials with default 5 (was 10; note DESIGN.md:1170 itself specifies check_space(space, rng, n=10), so the halved default is an implementation deviation from the design document, not a recorded decision). `measure` is gone: test vectors always come from space.random(rng=rng) (testing.py:115); REVIEW.md:74 (U 8) and review/r2_packaging_tests_docs.md:43 record this as an open, 'not done' item, not an agreed drop. New: rng argument (seedable), `rebuild` callable for an equality/hash check, dim>=0 check, self-equality and hashability (testing.py:90-109). The one-off checks (gram_schmidt, mean) now run after the loop instead of before. Components/basis/dual round trips are no longer part of this call; they live in check_coordinates. No header/footer printing. Fails with 'Axiom failed: <name>. <detail>' via _fail (testing.py:41). |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpaceAxiomChecks._check_vector_space_axioms` | Verifies (x + y) - y == x, a*(x + y) == a*x + a*y, and x + zero == x using add/subtract/multiply and `self.zero`. | `check_space, 'vector space axioms' block` | v1 checked (x+y)-y==x, a(x+y)==ax+ay, x+0==x on component arrays with np.allclose defaults. v2 checks commutativity, associativity, zero identity, negation (x + negative(x) == 0), scale(1,x)==x, scalar associativity, and both distributive laws (testing.py:119-153), compared in the space norm with rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12 via _assert_close. Lost: no identity exercises `subtract` directly (v1's (x+y)-y==x); subtract is only used inside _assert_close, so a wrong subtract would corrupt every residual rather than be named. Gained: five additional axioms, including negation and scalar associativity. |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpaceAxiomChecks._check_inner_product_axioms` | Verifies bilinearity in the first slot <a x + b y, z> == a<x,z> + b<y,z>, symmetry <x,y> == <y,x>, and the triangle inequality \|\|x+y\|\| <= \|\|x\|\| + \|\|y\|\|. | `check_space, 'inner product axioms' block` | Bilinearity is split into additivity <x+y,z>==<x,z>+<y,z> and homogeneity <ax,y>==a<x,y> (testing.py:161-170); symmetry retained (:156-160). New: positive-definiteness squared_norm(x)>0 (:171-175) and norm**2 == squared_norm (:176-180). Lost: the triangle inequality \|\|x+y\|\| <= \|\|x\|\|+\|\|y\|\| (grep 'triangle' pygeoinf2/testing.py: none). Scalar comparisons use _assert_scalar with rtol=1e-10 against max(\|a\|,\|b\|,1) rather than np.isclose defaults. |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpaceAxiomChecks._check_mapping_identities` | Verifies from_components(to_components(x)) reproduces the same components, and from_dual(to_dual(x)) reproduces x (compared through to_components). | `check_coordinates: 'the coordinate map round-trips', 'components round-trip', 'solve_gram inverts apply_gram'` | Moved from the space-level check into check_coordinates, so it runs only on CoordinateSpace. The component round trip is now checked both ways: from_components(to_components(x)) == x in the space norm (testing.py:271-273, stronger than v1's components-to-components compare) and to_components(from_components(c)) == c with np.allclose defaults (:274-275). Also new: components have shape (dim,) (:268-269), and additivity/homogeneity of to_components (:277-280). The dual round trip from_dual(to_dual(x)) == x is replaced by solve_gram(apply_gram(c)) == c with rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-10 (:289-292), because to_dual/from_dual were removed (DESIGN decision 1). |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpaceAxiomChecks._check_inplace_operations` | Verifies the in-place kernels: after `self.ax(a, x_copy)` the copy equals multiply(a, x); after `self.axpy(a, x, y_copy)` the copy equals add(multiply(a, x), y). | `check_space: 'axpy agrees with add and scale', 'scale_inplace agrees with scale' (return value only; mutation and identity untested)` | Same two identities, with ax renamed scale_inplace and multiply renamed scale, compared in the space norm (rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12) rather than np.allclose on components. But what is tested has narrowed: v2 compares only the RETURN VALUE of axpy/scale_inplace against the expected vector (testing.py:185-186,190-191) and never looks at `target` again, so neither `result is target` nor whether the argument was mutated at all is verified. v1 ignored the return value and inspected the mutated copy, i.e. it tested the in-place semantics themselves. Verified empirically (scratchpad/probe.py, re-run): a EuclideanSpace subclass whose axpy/scale_inplace return fresh arrays and leave their arguments untouched passes check_space(trials=20) while v1's .check() fails on it. This narrowing is design-consistent — DESIGN.md:1325-1329 makes the return value the contract because `Reals` is immutable — so it is deliberate, not a bug, but it is 'mutation no longer verified', not an added guarantee. Two v2 call sites still silently depend on mutation and would break on such a space: compat.py:150-152 (`self._space.axpy(a, x, y); return y`) and testing.py:196 itself (return of scale_inplace discarded). |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpaceAxiomChecks._check_gram_schmidt` | Draws min(dim, 5) samples via self.sampler, runs self.gram_schmidt on them, and verifies all pairwise inner products are 1 on the diagonal and 0 off it. | `check_space: 'gram_schmidt returns an orthonormal set'` | Draws min(dim, 3) vectors instead of min(dim, 5) (testing.py:200); pairwise inner products compared with rtol=1e-10 (_assert_scalar) instead of np.isclose defaults. Runs after the trial loop rather than before. The v1 try/except that printed and skipped on a ValueError from dependent samples is gone: a dependent draw now propagates gram_schmidt's ValueError (spaces.py:192-235, rtol=1e-12) and fails the check. Still skipped when dim == 0 (check_space returns early at :111). |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpaceAxiomChecks._check_basis_and_expectation` | For every i in range(dim), verifies to_components(basis_vector(i)) equals the unit vector e_i; then verifies sample_expectation of 5 samples equals the componentwise np.mean. | `check_coordinates 'basis_vector has the expected components' + check_space 'mean is the average of its arguments'` | Split in two. basis_vector: now in check_coordinates (CoordinateSpace only) and checks only i in range(min(dim, 4)) (testing.py:296-301) instead of every i in range(dim) — O(dim) rather than O(dim^2), an improvement on large spaces but no longer exhaustive. sample_expectation is renamed mean and checked in check_space with 4 samples against an explicit axpy(0.25, ...) accumulation compared in the norm (:210-216) rather than 5 samples against np.mean of component arrays; this is metric-free and works on non-coordinate spaces. |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpaceAxiomChecks.check.comparison_scheme` | Every HilbertSpace check compares vectors through their component arrays (not through the space's norm) and scalars with np.isclose, both at numpy's default rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8; the user cannot change tolerances. | `testing._assert_close / _assert_scalar` | check_space compares vectors in the space's own norm: residual > atol + rtol*max(\|\|a\|\|,\|\|b\|\|,1) with fixed rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12 (testing.py:45-58), and scalars with \|a-b\| > rtol*max(\|a\|,\|b\|,1), rtol=1e-10 (:61-66). This is metric-aware (v1 was component-based and metric-blind) and much tighter than numpy's 1e-5/1e-8. Tolerances remain non-configurable in check_space and check_coordinates (neither takes rtol/atol). check_coordinates still uses np.allclose with numpy defaults for the pure component identities (:274-288) and rtol=1e-8/atol=1e-10 for the Gram solve (:290). |
| `nonlinear_operators.NonLinearOperatorAxiomChecks` | Base mixin giving NonLinearOperator (and, through inheritance, LinearOperator and AffineOperator) a randomized `.check()` that validates the operator's derivative by finite differences and the derivative calculus rules (sum, scalar multiple, chain). | `testing.check_derivative, check_second_derivative, check_gradient (free functions)` | Mixin removed from Operator (no .check on pygeoinf2.algebra.operators.Operator, operators.py:211-445). The finite-difference derivative check survives as check_derivative(operator, point, rng=, step=, trials=, rtol=). The derivative-calculus rules (sum, scalar, chain) are no longer checked as identities; they are reachable only by finite-differencing the composite operator (see the per-rule rows). New in v2: check_second_derivative (testing.py:674-726; named check_hessian in DESIGN.md:1176) and check_gradient (:621-671), the latter being the metric-sensitive derivative-vs-gradient trap check. |
| `nonlinear_operators.NonLinearOperatorAxiomChecks.check` | Runs `n_checks` randomized trials: draws x, v from the domain (resampling v once if \|\|v\|\| < 1e-12) and a ~ randn(), then runs the finite-difference derivative check and the scalar-multiple rule; if `op2` is given also runs the sum rule and chain rule against op2. | `testing.check_derivative(operator, point, /, *, rng=None, step=1e-6, trials=3, rtol=1e-5) -> None` | op.check(n_checks=5, op2=None, check_rtol=1e-5, check_atol=1e-8, measure=None) becomes check_derivative(op, point, rng=, step=, trials=3, rtol=1e-5). The user must now supply the base point (v1 drew x per trial); trials default 3 not 5; only directions are randomised. Lost: op2 (no sum/chain rule), check_atol (no absolute tolerance at all), measure (REVIEW.md:74 U 8 'not done'). New: step keyword, rng Generator, and an explicit failure 'the operator carries a derivative' when has_derivative is False (testing.py:592-595) instead of propagating whatever derivative(x) raised. No printing. Directions normalised to unit norm (:602-603) instead of a single zero-norm resample. |
| `nonlinear_operators.NonLinearOperatorAxiomChecks._check_derivative_finite_difference` | Verifies derivative(x) is an instance of LinearOperator with domain/codomain equal to the operator's, then compares derivative(x)(v) against the forward difference (F(x + h v) - F(x)) / h in the codomain norm. | `check_derivative body (testing.py:597-618)` | Central differences (F(x+hd) - F(x-hd)) / 2h with step=1e-6 replace v1's forward difference with h=1e-7: truncation error O(h^2), two operator evaluations per direction (v1: F(x+hv) and F(x) — same count). Tolerance: residual > rtol*max(\|\|num\|\|,\|\|an\|\|,1) with rtol=1e-5 and NO 1e-4 floor (v1 clamped effective_rtol to >= 1e-4) and no atol term; the max(...,1) gives an implicit absolute floor of rtol. The derivative is taken from operator.at(point).derivative (:598-599), exercising the linearise path. LOST: v1's assertions that derivative(x) is a LinearOperator instance and that its domain/codomain equal the operator's (v1 :27-33); grep 'isinstance(.*LinearOperator' pygeoinf2/testing.py: none. |
| `nonlinear_operators.NonLinearOperatorAxiomChecks.check.failure_criterion` | All operator-level checks (non-linear, linear, affine) compare results in the codomain (or domain) norm of the Hilbert space and only raise when the discrepancy exceeds BOTH the absolute and the relative tolerance; satisfying either one passes. | `testing._assert_close / _assert_scalar and the inline criteria in check_derivative/check_gradient/check_second_derivative` | Still norm-based and metric-aware, but the rule changed from 'fail iff diff > atol AND diff > rtol*(\|\|ref\|\|+1e-12)' (either tolerance passes) to the additive numpy-style 'fail iff residual > atol + rtol*scale' with scale = max(\|\|a\|\|,\|\|b\|\|,1.0) (testing.py:55-57) — the max(...,1) means every check carries an implicit absolute floor of rtol*1 in the space's units, and the reference is the larger of the two sides rather than the second argument. check_derivative/check_gradient/check_second_derivative use residual > rtol*scale with no atol (:612-614,:664-665,:720-722). Scalars: \|a-b\| > rtol*max(\|a\|,\|b\|,1) (:64-65). Tolerances are fixed per function (1e-10/1e-12 for vectors, 1e-9 for adjoint scalars) except the rtol keyword on the three derivative checks. |
| `nonlinear_operators.NonLinearOperatorAxiomChecks.check.sampling` | Random test vectors come from `domain.random()` by default or from a user-supplied GaussianMeasure on the domain; scalars come from np.random.randn(). | `domain.random(rng=rng) with rng: numpy.random.Generator; scalars from rng.normal()` | Every check takes `rng: Generator \| None` and defaults to default_rng() (testing.py:591), so runs are reproducible — an improvement over v1's global RNG. LOST: sampling from a user-supplied GaussianMeasure (`measure`, `domain_measure`, `codomain_measure`); grep 'measure' in testing.py hits only check_measure's argument. REVIEW.md:74 item 8, review/r2_packaging_tests_docs.md:43 (U 8) and REVIEW2.md:135 record this as an open regression needed by pyslfp (smooth test fields), not an agreed drop; review/pyslfp_usage.md:182 proposes restoring it as domain_measure/codomain_measure or a `sampler` argument, and no such name exists in testing.py. The zero-norm resample is replaced by normalising the direction with a 1e-30 floor (:602-603). |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperatorAxiomChecks` | Mixin extending the non-linear checks with linearity, the adjoint identity <L x, y> = <x, L* y>, and (given a second operator) algebraic identities for adjoint and dual. | `testing.check_operator + testing.check_traits (free functions)` | Mixin removed; check_operator(op, rng=, trials=5) keeps linearity and the adjoint identity and adds three structural adjoint checks (right spaces, memoised, involutive). The two-operator adjoint algebra and the dual identity are not checked as identities (see their rows); no non-linear derivative checks run automatically (contrary to DESIGN.md:1172, which lists 'derivative by finite differences' under check_operator). New: check_traits verifies claimed traits (SELF_ADJOINT, POSITIVE_(SEMI)DEFINITE, ISOMETRY, IDEMPOTENT, UNITARY, INVERTIBLE) — no v1 counterpart. |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperatorAxiomChecks.check` | Override: first runs the inherited non-linear checks (with measure=domain_measure), then `n_checks` further trials drawing x1, x2 from the domain and y from the codomain to verify linearity and the adjoint identity; with `op2` also verifies the adjoint/dual algebraic identities. | `testing.check_operator(operator, /, *, rng=None, trials=5) -> None` | op.check(n_checks=5, op2=None, check_rtol=1e-5, check_atol=1e-8, domain_measure=None, codomain_measure=None) becomes check_operator(op, rng=, trials=5). Lost: op2 (adjoint/dual algebra), check_rtol/check_atol (fixed at rtol=1e-10/atol=1e-12 for linearity, rtol=1e-9 for the adjoint scalar), domain_measure/codomain_measure (REVIEW.md:74 U 8, open). Does not run the finite-difference derivative check first (v1 super().check()), although DESIGN.md:1172 specified that it would. New: asserts adjoint.domain/codomain are the swapped spaces (testing.py:446-451), `operator.adjoint is adjoint` memoisation (:452-453), and `adjoint.adjoint is operator` involution by identity (:454-455). No printing; seedable rng. |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperatorAxiomChecks._check_linearity` | Verifies L(a x + b y) equals a L(x) + b L(y) by comparing in the codomain norm. | `check_operator: 'the operator is linear'` | Same identity L(ax+by) == aL(x)+bL(y) with three applications per trial, compared in the codomain norm (testing.py:438-444). Criterion changed to residual > 1e-12 + 1e-10*max(\|\|lhs\|\|,\|\|rhs\|\|,1) (fixed, not user-settable) from v1's both-must-exceed with user rtol=1e-5/atol=1e-8. |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperatorAxiomChecks._check_adjoint_definition` | Verifies codomain.inner_product(L(x), y) == domain.inner_product(x, L.adjoint(y)) as scalars. | `check_operator: 'the adjoint satisfies (A x, y) == (x, A* y)'` | Same metric-sensitive identity codomain.inner_product(A x, y) == domain.inner_product(x, A* y) with x from the domain and y from the codomain (testing.py:457-464). Criterion: \|lhs-rhs\| > 1e-9*max(\|lhs\|,\|rhs\|,1) (fixed rtol=1e-9, no atol keyword) instead of np.isclose(lhs, rhs, rtol=check_rtol, atol=check_atol). Tolerances not configurable. |

### data_assimilation — `data_assimilation/`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `core.global_rng_usage` | Two different RNG conventions coexist: ProbabilityGrid.sample uses a fresh unseeded np.random.default_rng(), while GaussianLikelihood.sample, EnsembleKalmanFilter (initial ensemble and perturbations) and generate_synthetic_data(seed=...) use the legacy global np.random state. | `rng: numpy.random.Generator \| None keyword on every sampling method` | Where v1 mixed a fresh unseeded default_rng (ProbabilityGrid.sample) with the legacy global np.random state (GaussianLikelihood.sample, EnKF, generate_synthetic_data(seed=)), every v2 replacement takes an explicit rng= Generator: ProbabilityMeasure.sample(rng=), samples(n, rng=, n_jobs=) which spawns one child stream per draw, GaussianMeasure.sample(rng=), ForwardProblem.synthetic_data(rng=). np.random.seed has no effect anywhere; reproducibility is rng=np.random.default_rng(seed). No seed= keyword exists outside tests (backends/mfem.py:726 derives an int seed from an rng, not a user-facing seed=). |

## 4. Subsumed (reached differently)

### hilbert_space — `hilbert_space.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpace.to_dual` | Maps a vector to its canonical dual vector (a LinearForm) — the Riesz map primal->dual, which together with from_dual defines the inner product. | `LinearFunctional.from_representer(space, x) for the functional; `space.apply_gram(space.to_components(x))` for what v1 called its components (CoordinateSpace only)` | No dual space and no LinearForm. The functional pairing with x is `LinearFunctional.from_representer(space, x)` (operators.py:2237-2239); its derivative components (= v1 to_dual(x).components = G c_x) are `space.apply_gram(space.to_components(x))` (spaces.py:356-358 default identity, DiagonalMetricSpace 995-997) or `f.derivative_components` (operators.py:2165-2175). compat.py:179-186 documents the identity. On a coordinate-free space only the functional form exists. |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpace.from_dual` | Maps a dual vector (LinearForm) back to its primal representative; the inverse Riesz map. | `CoordinateSpace.representer(derivative_components) ; LinearFunctional.representer (= f.adjoint(1.0))` | For a functional object: `f.representer` (operators.py:2142-2148, cached). For a component array g in the derivative convention: `space.representer(g)` = from_components(solve_gram(g)) (spaces.py:722-730), CoordinateSpace only. Also `space.coordinate_projection().adjoint` is the same map as an operator (687-703). |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpace.duality_product` | Duality pairing <xp, x>, evaluated as xp(x). | `f(x) on a LinearFunctional; `float(g @ space.to_components(x))` for derivative components g` | No pairing method on the space. Evaluate the functional directly (`f(x)`, LinearFunctional is an Operator), or pair derivative components with components by np.dot (the identity testing.check_representer uses, testing.py:337-341). |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpace.riesz` | The Riesz map dual->primal as a LinearOperator, built via LinearOperator.self_dual(self.dual, self.from_dual). | `space.coordinate_projection().adjoint  (EuclideanSpace(dim) of derivative components -> space), or space.representer(g) as a function` | No Riesz operator object, since there is no dual space for it to map from. The same linear map, with the 'dual' realised as derivative-component arrays in EuclideanSpace(dim), is `space.coordinate_projection().adjoint` (adjoint = representer = from_components∘solve_gram, spaces.py:687-703, 722-730). CoordinateSpace only; matrix-free. |
| `hilbert_space.HilbertSpace.inverse_riesz` | The inverse Riesz map primal->dual as a LinearOperator, built via LinearOperator.self_dual(self, self.to_dual). | `space.coordinate_inclusion().adjoint  (space -> EuclideanSpace(dim) derivative components); or LinearFunctional.from_representer(space, x).derivative_components` | Same map as v1 (x -> G c_x) available as the adjoint of coordinate_inclusion (spaces.py:705-720) or via `f.derivative_components` (operators.py:2165-2175). CoordinateSpace only; no self-dual operator object. |
| `hilbert_space.DualHilbertSpace.to_dual` | Maps a dual vector (LinearForm) to a primal vector via underlying_space.from_dual. | `f.representer  (LinearFunctional property, = f.adjoint(1.0))` | Mapping a functional to its primal representative is `f.representer` (operators.py:2142-2148; cached). No dual-space object involved. |
| `hilbert_space.DualHilbertSpace.from_dual` | Maps a primal vector to a LinearForm via underlying_space.to_dual. | `LinearFunctional.from_representer(space, x)` | Mapping a primal vector to the functional pairing with it is `LinearFunctional.from_representer(space, x)` (operators.py:2237-2239, `_RepresenterFunctional`). Works on coordinate-free spaces too. |
| `hilbert_space.DualHilbertSpace.to_components` | Returns x.components of the LinearForm. | `f.derivative_components  (= G c_representer)` | `LinearFunctional.derivative_components` returns the array g with f(x) = g . c_x (operators.py:2165-2175), which is what v1's LinearForm.components / DualHilbertSpace.to_components returned. Requires a CoordinateSpace domain (require_coordinates). |
| `hilbert_space.DualHilbertSpace.from_components` | Builds LinearForm(underlying_space, components=c). | `LinearFunctional.from_derivative_components(space, g)` | Builds the functional x -> g . c_x from derivative components (operators.py:2242-2267), applying solve_gram once to store the representer; raises ValueError on wrong shape (v1 did not validate). CoordinateSpace only. |
| `hilbert_space.DualHilbertSpace.duality_product` | Evaluates x(xp): here `x` is the primal vector and `xp` the LinearForm, keeping the base signature but reversing the roles. | `f(x)` | The reversed-role pairing existed only to make inner products on the dual space work; in v2 one evaluates the functional directly. (Inner products between functionals: `space.inner_product(f.representer, g.representer)`.) |
| `hilbert_space.OrthogonalHilbertSpace.metric` | The metric tensor as a sparse CSR diagonal matrix. | `space.apply_gram(c) / space.apply_gram_to_columns(C) for the action; `scipy.sparse.diags(space.metric_values, format='csr')` if the sparse object itself is wanted` | The library no longer hands out a ready-made sparse matrix. Metric application is `apply_gram` (pointwise multiply, spaces.py:995-997) or `apply_gram_to_columns` (1003-1005). The only matrix the library offers is dense `gram_matrix()`, which DiagonalMetricSpace does NOT override, so it forms an n x n dense array by n apply_gram calls (400-408; review/r2_algebra_solvers.md:27 'A Consider-15 gram_matrix overrides \| not done'). A user wanting a sparse matrix builds it from metric_values (as inference/preconditioners.py:535 does internally). |
| `hilbert_space.OrthogonalHilbertSpace.inverse_metric` | The inverse metric tensor as a sparse CSR diagonal matrix (1/metric_values). | `space.solve_gram(c) / space.solve_gram_to_columns(C); `scipy.sparse.diags(1.0/space.metric_values)` by hand` | Same situation as `metric`: action only (pointwise divide, spaces.py:999-1001, 1007-1009); no sparse object supplied. |
| `hilbert_space.OrthogonalHilbertSpace.to_dual` | Riesz map: LinearForm(self, components=to_components(x) * metric_values). | `space.apply_gram(space.to_components(x))  (components); LinearFunctional.from_representer(space, x)  (functional)` | The O(n) pointwise scaling survives as apply_gram = metric_values * c (spaces.py:995-997). No LinearForm is produced. |
| `hilbert_space.OrthogonalHilbertSpace.from_dual` | Inverse Riesz map: from_components(xp.components / metric_values). | `space.representer(g) = from_components(g / metric_values)` | representer (spaces.py:722-730) composed with DiagonalMetricSpace.solve_gram (999-1001) gives exactly v1's from_components(components / metric_values), O(n). |
| `hilbert_space.OrthonormalHilbertSpace.to_dual` | LinearForm(self, components=to_components(x)) — no scaling. | `space.to_components(x) (apply_gram is the identity); LinearFunctional.from_representer(space, x)` | No scaling, as in v1; apply_gram is the inherited identity (spaces.py:356-358). No LinearForm object. |
| `hilbert_space.OrthonormalHilbertSpace.from_dual` | from_components(xp.components) — no scaling. | `space.representer(c) = from_components(c)` | representer with the identity solve_gram (spaces.py:360-362, 722-730) is v1's from_components(xp.components). |
| `hilbert_space.MassWeightedHilbertSpace.to_dual` | R_Y(x) = R_X(M x): applies the mass operator, maps through the underlying Riesz map, and re-wraps the components as a LinearForm on this space. | `LinearFunctional.from_representer(weighted, x); components: weighted.base.apply_gram(weighted.base.to_components(weighted.mass(x)))` | R_Y(x) = R_X(M x) has no method; the functional is from_representer (operators.py:2237) whose value is `weighted.inner_product(x, .)` = base.inner_product(mass(x), .) (spaces.py:933-935). Its derivative components must be assembled by hand through the base (the weighted space lacks apply_gram). |
| `hilbert_space.MassWeightedHilbertSpace.from_dual` | R_Y^{-1}(xp) = M^{-1} R_X^{-1}(xp): passes the form straight to the underlying from_dual, then applies the inverse mass operator. | `f.representer (= f.adjoint(1.0)) for a functional on the weighted space; for derivative components g: weighted.mass_inverse(weighted.base.representer(g))` | R_Y^{-1} = M^{-1} R_X^{-1} survives as the composition above (spaces.py:886-896, 722-730); no method on the weighted space since it is not a CoordinateSpace, and `LinearFunctional.from_derivative_components(weighted, g)` is refused by require_coordinates (operators.py:2260). |
| `hilbert_space.MassWeightedHilbertModule.vector_multiply` | Delegates to underlying_space.vector_multiply. | `weighted.base.multiply(x, y)  (when base is a HilbertModule; vectors are shared)` | No method on the weighted space; because MassWeightedSpace holds the base's vectors (spaces.py:915-923) the base's pointwise product applies to them. But code that checks `isinstance(space, HilbertModule)` / `require_module(space)` on the weighted space fails (780-799). Reachable only by stepping outside the weighted space; the parent-class row is 'lost' for that reason. |
| `hilbert_space.MassWeightedHilbertModule.vector_sqrt` | Delegates to underlying_space.vector_sqrt. | `weighted.base.sqrt(x)` | As for vector_multiply: only through the base. |

### operators — `linear_operators.py, linear_forms.py, nonlinear_forms.py, nonlinear_operators.py, affine_operators.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `linear_forms.LinearForm.from_linear_operator` | Builds a LinearForm from an operator whose codomain is EuclideanSpace(1), via mapping x -> operator(x)[0]. | `LinearFunctional.from_callables(domain, lambda x: op(x)[0], representer=lambda: op.adjoint(np.ones(1)))` | No converter exists; a LinearOperator into Reals built with LinearOperator.from_callables is NOT a LinearFunctional (probe: isinstance False). Wrap explicitly as in the v2 call (or for an op into Reals: representer=lambda: op.adjoint(1.0)). Components are not probed serially any more; the representer comes from the adjoint. |
| `linear_forms.LinearForm.as_linear_operator` | Wraps the form as a LinearOperator domain -> EuclideanSpace(1) with mapping x -> np.array([f(x)]) and dual_mapping y -> y * f. | `the LinearFunctional itself (isinstance(f, LinearOperator) is True; codomain is Reals, not EuclideanSpace(1))` | LinearFunctional subclasses LinearOperator, so no wrapper is needed; values are floats rather than 1-arrays. |
| `linear_forms.LinearForm.copy` | Returns a new LinearForm with a copied components array. | `not needed: operators are immutable; f.with_traits(Traits.NONE) yields a shallow clone if an independent object is wanted` | No copy() method; grep 'def copy' in algebra/operators.py finds none. Immutability (with_traits docstring) removes the reason for it. |
| `linear_forms.LinearForm.component_computation` | When built from a mapping, components[i] = mapping(e_i) for each basis vector: serial branch builds e_i via domain.from_components on a unit array; parallel branch uses joblib Parallel(n_jobs) with domain.basis_vector(i) per worker. | `LinearFunctional.from_callables(domain, f, derivative_components=lambda: LinearOperator.from_callables(domain, Reals(), f).matrix(by='columns', n_jobs=n_jobs)[0])` | No constructor probes basis vectors for you. The probe must be written explicitly: either the matrix() route above (parallel via n_jobs, one basis vector per column; probe confirmed returns [[1,1,1]] for the sum functional) or np.array([f(domain.basis_vector(i)) for i in range(domain.dim)]). joblib parallel= on the form constructor is gone. |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperator.from_formally_self_adjoint` | Promotes a formally self-adjoint operator on an underlying space to a self-adjoint operator on the weighted space; equals from_formal_adjoint(domain, domain, operator). | `LinearOperator.from_formal_adjoint(domain, domain, operator, traits=Traits.SELF_ADJOINT) (or lift_formal_adjoint(operator, domain, traits=...))` | No separate constructor, and self-adjointness is no longer claimed automatically -- the docstring argues it holds only if the operator commutes with the metric ratio. Claim it via traits and verify with check_traits. |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperator.from_linear_forms` | Builds an operator forms[0].domain -> EuclideanSpace(len(forms)) whose i-th output is forms[i](x), by stacking the forms' component vectors into a dense (N x dim) matrix. | `LinearOperator.from_matrix(forms[0].domain, EuclideanSpace(len(forms)), np.stack([f.derivative_components for f in forms]), form='components')` | No stacking constructor in the core. Build the (N x dim) row matrix from each LinearFunctional's derivative_components and hand it to from_matrix (codomain Euclidean, so components and Galerkin forms coincide). Requires a CoordinateSpace domain. Alternatives: ColumnLinearOperator in algebra/direct_sum.py (stacks x -> (f1(x), f2(x), ...) with a DirectSum(Reals, ...) codomain, not R^N; RowLinearOperator is the other shape -- DirectSum domain, shared codomain; Review A evidence fix, confirmed at direct_sum.py:665/747); backends.mfem_hilbert.operator_from_linear_forms for MFEM load vectors. The catalogue's named target from_derivative_matrix does not exist (renamed to from_matrix by D-4). |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperator.from_linear_form` | Rank-1 operator form.domain -> EuclideanSpace(1): x -> [form(x)], dual y' -> (codomain.from_dual(y')[0]) * form via domain.dual.multiply. | `the LinearFunctional itself (already a LinearOperator into Reals); for an R^1 codomain use LinearOperator.from_vectors(domain, [f.representer]).adjoint` | A LinearFunctional is a LinearOperator, so no rank-1 wrapper is needed; codomain is Reals (floats) rather than EuclideanSpace(1). |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperator.from_vector` | Rank-1 operator domain -> EuclideanSpace(1): x -> [<vector, x>]; adjoint y -> domain.multiply(y[0], vector). | `LinearFunctional.from_representer(domain, v) (into Reals), or LinearOperator.from_vectors(domain, [v]).adjoint (into EuclideanSpace(1))` | No rank-1 constructor by name; both routes give x -> (v, x) with adjoint t -> t v. |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperator.self_adjoint_from_matrix` | Same type dispatch as from_matrix but with codomain = domain and galerkin=True always; user is responsible for symmetry of the matrix. | `LinearOperator.from_matrix(domain, domain, matrix, form='galerkin', traits=Traits.SELF_ADJOINT)` | Merged into from_matrix (D-4). The user now states both the form and the self-adjointness claim; symmetry still unchecked at construction (check_traits verifies). |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperator.self_adjoint_from_tensor_product` | Self-adjoint operator A(x) = sum_i w_i <v_i, x> v_i built via LinearOperator.self_adjoint. | `U = LinearOperator.from_vectors(domain, vectors); U @ DiagonalLinearOperator(EuclideanSpace(len(vectors)), weights) @ U.adjoint` | No named constructor. The composition is recognised as SELF_ADJOINT\|POSITIVE_SEMIDEFINITE by the adjoint-palindrome rule (probe confirmed traits), so the self-adjoint claim comes for free; a single vector can use from_tensor_product(v, v, ...). |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperator.linear` | Always True; marker distinguishing linear operators. | `isinstance(op, LinearOperator)` | No boolean property; linearity is type-level. grep 'def linear' in operators.py finds nothing. |
| `linear_operators.LinearOperator.default_dual_derivation` | If neither dual_mapping nor adjoint_mapping is given, the dual is defined as yp -> LinearForm(domain, mapping=lambda x: yp(A(x))), which computes components by applying A to every basis vector (O(dim) operator applications per dual/adjoint application); the adjoint is then derived through to_dual/from_dual. | `LinearOperator.from_matrix(A.domain, A.codomain, A.matrix(by='columns'), form='components').adjoint (explicit assembly)` | Not automatic any more: _CallableLinearOperator._adjoint_value raises NotImplementedError when no adjoint was supplied (probe confirmed). The docstring of from_callables (1066-1069: 'Without it the adjoint is derived by solving') contradicts the code. The v1 capability (correct O(dim)-per-application adjoint for small problems) is reachable only by assembling the components matrix by columns and taking the adjoint of the MatrixLinearOperator (A.assembled() itself may fail because by='auto' can choose rows). |
| `linear_operators.MatrixLinearOperator.is_dense` | True if the stored matrix is a NumPy ndarray. | `not scipy.sparse.issparse(op.stored_matrix)` | No property; test the stored array's type. |
| `linear_operators.MatrixLinearOperator.is_galerkin` | True if the stored matrix is the Galerkin representation. | `op.stored_form == 'galerkin'` | Renamed to a string-valued stored_form property. |
| `linear_operators.DenseMatrixLinearOperator` | MatrixLinearOperator specialised to a dense NumPy matrix; the result type of with_dense_matrix and of from_matrix for ndarray inputs. | `MatrixLinearOperator with an np.ndarray (LinearOperator.from_matrix(..., form=...) or op.assembled())` | No dense-only subclass; MatrixLinearOperator covers it. No 'Matrix must be input in dense form' check since sparse is equally accepted. |
| `linear_operators.SparseMatrixLinearOperator` | MatrixLinearOperator backed by a modern SciPy sparse array, converted to CSR on construction; delegates diagonal extraction and densification to SciPy routines. | `LinearOperator.from_matrix(domain, codomain, sparse_matrix, form=...) -> MatrixLinearOperator keeping the sparse array` | No separate class. Sparse input is kept as given (no CSR conversion; a dia_array stays dia_array, probe confirmed), legacy spmatrix accepted (issparse). Action is stored @ c; adjoint stored.T @ c; apply_block one sparse product; diagonals read via .diagonal(k) without densifying when the form matches. |
| `linear_operators.SparseMatrixLinearOperator.sparse_array` | Read access to the underlying CSR sparse array. | `MatrixLinearOperator.stored_matrix` | Renamed and generalised (dense or sparse). Returns the internal object (read-only by convention), as v1 did. |
| `linear_operators.DiagonalSparseMatrixLinearOperator.from_operator` | Diagonal (banded) approximation of any LinearOperator: calls operator.extract_diagonals(offsets, galerkin=galerkin) and wraps the result. | `d = A.diagonals(offsets=offsets, form='galerkin'); LinearOperator.from_matrix(A.domain, A.codomain, scipy.sparse.dia_array((d, offsets), shape=(A.codomain.dim, A.domain.dim)), form='galerkin')  (exactly what numerics.preconditioners.BandedPreconditioner._invert does); for offset 0 only: DiagonalLinearOperator(A.domain, A.diagonals(form='components')[0])` | No classmethod; the banded approximation is assembled by hand from diagonals(). diagonals() now accepts n_jobs and probe='banded' (v1's from_operator exposed neither parallel nor n_jobs). Default form is 'auto' rather than v1's galerkin=True. |
| `linear_operators.DiagonalSparseMatrixLinearOperator.offsets` | The array of stored diagonal offsets (from the dia_array). | `op.stored_matrix.offsets (dia_array-backed MatrixLinearOperator); DiagonalLinearOperator has only offset 0` | No property; read it off the stored scipy dia_array. |
| `linear_operators.DiagonalSparseMatrixLinearOperator.is_strictly_diagonal` | True if the only stored diagonal is the main one (offsets == [0]). | `isinstance(op, DiagonalLinearOperator) (or list(op.stored_matrix.offsets) == [0] for a dia-backed MatrixLinearOperator)` | Strict diagonality is now a class, which is what gates the functional calculus. |

### direct_sum — `direct_sum.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `direct_sum.HilbertSpaceDirectSum.number_of_subspaces` | Number of component subspaces. | `len(S) or len(S.subspaces)` | No number_of_subspaces property; DirectSum defines __len__, so the count is len(S) (or len(S.subspaces)). |
| `direct_sum.BlockStructure` | Abstract base (ABC) mixin for operators with a block structure: records the number of block rows and columns and declares the abstract block(i, j) accessor. | `BlockOperator.row_dim / col_dim / block / blocks; ColumnOperator.operators, RowOperator.operators, BlockDiagonalOperator.operators` | No abstract mixin. Only BlockOperator/BlockLinearOperator expose row_dim, col_dim and block(i, j); Column/Row/BlockDiagonal expose the sequence as `.operators` (so i-th block is op.operators[i], count is len(op.operators)). No common interface across the four classes, and no shared index validation. |
| `direct_sum.ColumnLinearOperator.block` | Returns the i-th operator; j must be 0. | `op.operators[i]` | No block(i, j) on ColumnOperator/ColumnLinearOperator; the i-th block is op.operators[i] (tuple indexing, IndexError on out-of-range). No validation of j. |
| `direct_sum.RowLinearOperator.block` | Returns the j-th operator; i must be 0. | `op.operators[j]` | No block(i, j) on RowOperator/RowLinearOperator; the j-th block is op.operators[j]. No validation of i. |
| `direct_sum.BlockDiagonalLinearOperator.block` | Returns the i-th diagonal operator when i == j; otherwise a zero operator from operators[j].domain to operators[i].codomain. | `op.operators[i] for i == j; LinearOperator.zero(op.operators[j].domain, codomain=op.operators[i].codomain) for i != j` | No block(i, j) accessor. Diagonal blocks via op.operators[i]; an off-diagonal zero block must be built by the user with LinearOperator.zero(domain, codomain=) (v1 used domain.zero_operator(codomain), also gone). The same synthesis is done internally in _known_matrix (:841-851). |

### linear_solvers — `linear_solvers.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `linear_solvers.DirectLinearSolver._build_inverse_operator` | Shared wrapping scheme used by all direct solvers: given component-array solve and adjoint-solve callables, builds the inverse LinearOperator (codomain -> domain) with an adjoint. | `DirectSolver._invert + InverseOperator` | Replaced by `DirectSolver._invert(operator)` (solvers.py:458-520), which obtains `(apply_inverse, apply_transposed)` from the abstract `_factorise(matrix)` and builds an `InverseOperator(operator, self, solve_fn, adjoint_solve_fn=..., known_matrix=..., components_action=..., components_adjoint_action=...)`. The Galerkin branch's to_dual/from_components dance is now `codomain.apply_gram(cy)` before the solve (:466-468); the non-Galerkin branch no longer wraps a scipy LinearOperator in `from_matrix` — the inverse exposes a `components_action` instead. Adjoint solve carries the metric explicitly (:498-507). If `apply_transposed` is None and the operator is not SELF_ADJOINT the adjoint is rebuilt by `self._solver(self._operator.adjoint)` (:354), i.e. refactorised; v1 reused the forward solve for the adjoint by default. IMPROVED: `known_matrix` lets `inverse.matrix()` be produced from the factors without dim solves (:472-481). |
| `linear_solvers.ScipyIterativeSolver.callback_and_iteration_counting` | A user callback passed via kwargs is wrapped in an internal counter that increments `iterations` on every SciPy callback invocation and then forwards *args to the user callback; the wrapper always replaces the callback key in the kwargs given to SciPy. | `IterativeSolver(callback=(iteration, residual)) + SolveResult.iterations/history` | Iteration counting is now `solver(A).solve(y).iterations`; a live callback is `IterativeSolver(callback=lambda i, r: ...)`, invoked by `_record` on every step of every iterative solver with the residual norm. The SciPy-specific pieces (pr_norm callback_type default for gmres, *args passthrough, reset/finalize duck typing) have no equivalent. |
| `linear_solvers.CGMatrixSolver` | Factory returning `ScipyIterativeSolver('cg', galerkin=galerkin, **kwargs)`. | `pygeoinf2.numerics.solvers.CGSolver` | Use `CGSolver(rtol=..., atol=..., maxiter=..., preconditioner=..., callback=...)(A)`. On a coordinate space the loop runs on component arrays via ComponentView with the space's metric, so it is as matrix-level as SciPy's cg without the Galerkin flag. SciPy kwargs pass-through (callback_type etc.) is gone; requires the operator to claim POSITIVE_DEFINITE. |
| `linear_solvers.BICGStabMatrixSolver` | Factory returning `ScipyIterativeSolver('bicgstab', galerkin=galerkin, **kwargs)`. | `pygeoinf2.numerics.solvers.BiCGStabSolver` | Use `BiCGStabSolver(rtol=..., maxiter=..., preconditioner=...)(A)`; runs on components when coordinates exist. No SciPy kwargs pass-through. |
| `linear_solvers.GMRESMatrixSolver` | Factory returning `ScipyIterativeSolver('gmres', galerkin=galerkin, **kwargs)`. | `pygeoinf2.numerics.solvers.GMRESSolver` | Use `GMRESSolver(restart=30, rtol=..., maxiter=..., preconditioner=...)(A)` — a native, coordinate-free, left-preconditioned restarted GMRES (Arnoldi + Givens). `restart` is a constructor kwarg (validated > 0). Residual reported is the preconditioned one when a preconditioner is set (:1086-1088). |
| `linear_solvers.ProgressCallback.message` | Text prefix printed before the iteration number. | `ProgressCallback(report=...)` | No `message` attribute. The line text is fixed; customise output by supplying `ProgressCallback(report=lambda line: print('Iteration: ' + line, end='\r'))` — the report callable receives the formatted line and may rewrite it. |

### preconditioners — `preconditioners.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `preconditioners.IterativePreconditioningMethod` | Wraps an iterative solver so that a few loose inner iterations act as a preconditioner; documented as best used with FCGSolver (flexible CG) because the inner action varies between calls. | `Pass an IterativeSolver directly as the preconditioner: FlexibleCGSolver(rtol=1e-8, preconditioner=CGSolver(rtol=1e-1, maxiter=5, strict=False))  or  CGSolver(...).with_preconditioner(CGSolver(rtol=1e-1, maxiter=5, strict=False))` | No class named Iterative* exists in v2 (grep 'IterativePreconditioning\|IterativePreconditioner\|inner_solver\|max_inner_iter' over pygeoinf2/**/*.py and *.md: no v2 class; only DESIGN.md:3426 and V1_CATALOGUE.md:152 mention it, and the only '_inner_solver' hits are WoodburyPreconditioner's private default, a different capability). The capability is reachable because IterativeSolver accepts `preconditioner: LinearSolver \| LinearOperator` and, when given a LinearSolver, calls it on the operator at solve time (solvers.py:793-800), and every IterativeSolver is a LinearSolver whose __call__ returns an InverseOperator whose action is 'solve the system'. Confirmed at runtime: both constructions converge on a 30-dim SPD operator (18 outer iterations, relative residual 8.5e-9). Differences: the inner iteration cap and tolerance are set on the inner solver's constructor (maxiter=, rtol=) rather than by a wrapper with defaults 5 / 1e-1; `strict=False` is REQUIRED because v2 iterative solvers raise ConvergenceError by default when maxiter is hit (solvers.py:820-832) — v1 never raised; and with strict=False every non-converged inner solve emits a RuntimeWarning (solvers.py:829-831), i.e. one warning per outer iteration for a deliberately loose inner solve (measured: 36 RuntimeWarnings across two solves; tests/test_phase_four.py:214 has to wrap it in pytest.warns). FlexibleCGSolver (v1 FCGSolver) exists and is exported. TEST COVERAGE GAP: no v2 test passes a bare IterativeSolver as preconditioner= — the cited demonstration wraps the inner InverseOperator in LinearOperator.from_callables first — so the direct LinearSolver-as-preconditioner path is exercised only by the reviewer's runtime check. |
| `preconditioners.IterativePreconditioningMethod.__call__` | Overrides the inner solver's iteration cap and tolerance, then returns inner_solver(operator), i.e. the InverseLinearOperator whose action is 'solve the system'. | `IterativeSolver.__call__(operator) -> InverseOperator, invoked by IterativeSolver._resolve_preconditioner when the attached preconditioner is a LinearSolver` | Equivalent action: the inner IterativeSolver's __call__ runs _validate then _invert and returns an InverseOperator whose _value runs the inner Krylov solve on each application (solvers.py:834-862). No override of the inner settings happens (see mutation row). The outer solver builds it once per outer __call__ (solvers.py:835) — same timing as v1's preconditioning_method(operator) (v1 linear_solvers.py:306). |
| `preconditioners.IterativePreconditioningMethod.inner_solver_mutation` | Each __call__ overwrites the passed inner solver's _maxiter and _rtol attributes in place (default 5 iterations, rtol 1e-1) rather than copying the solver, so the user's solver object is permanently altered. | `Construct the inner solver with the wanted settings: CGSolver(rtol=1e-1, maxiter=5, strict=False)` | The in-place overwrite of the inner solver's private _maxiter/_rtol is gone (there is no wrapper to do it), which removes the side effect on the user's solver object — an improvement — but the defaults it supplied (max_inner_iter=5, rtol=1e-1) are no longer supplied by anything: a user must set maxiter=/rtol=/strict=False on the inner solver explicitly, or the inner CG runs to its own defaults (rtol=1e-8, maxiter=max(2*dim,20), strict=True — which would raise on failure and is not a cheap preconditioner). v2 IterativeSolver still stores _rtol/_maxiter under the same private names (solvers.py:721-723) so the v1 mutation could be reproduced by hand, but nothing in v2 does it. |

### low_rank — `low_rank.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `low_rank.MatrixLike` | Module-level type alias for objects that act like matrices: a numpy ndarray or a scipy.sparse.linalg.LinearOperator. | `(none) -- LinearOperator.from_matrix(EuclideanSpace(n), EuclideanSpace(n), array, form="components") / LinearOperator.from_callables(domain, codomain, matvec, adjoint=rmatvec)` | The type alias is gone (grep 'MatrixLike\|ScipyLinOp\|aslinearoperator' over pygeoinf2/*.py: no hits outside backends/mfem.py and the preconditioners' sparse imports). Its only role was annotating the ndarray-or-scipy-LinearOperator input of random_diagonal and the component range finders; in v2 every randomised routine takes a pygeoinf2 LinearOperator. A user with a raw ndarray writes `random_diagonal(LinearOperator.from_matrix(EuclideanSpace(n), EuclideanSpace(n), M, form="components"), samples=...)`; a scipy LinearOperator must be wrapped by hand with LinearOperator.from_callables(domain, codomain, matvec, adjoint=rmatvec) -- domain and codomain are required positionals -- there is no aslinearoperator-style adapter. |
| `low_rank.white_noise_measure` | Creates a formal N(0, I) white-noise GaussianMeasure on the given domain, used as a numerical tool to generate isotropic test vectors that respect the domain's inner product (mass matrix). | `GaussianMeasure.from_standard_deviation(domain, 1.0) (probe role: HilbertSpace.white_noise(rng=))` | The named wrapper is gone (grep 'white_noise_measure' in pygeoinf2: only the randomised.py module docstring and tests/test_compat.py which imports v1's), but its entire v1 body was `return GaussianMeasure.from_standard_deviation(domain, 1.0)` (low_rank.py:47), and that call exists in v2 with the same positional signature (domain, standard_deviation, /, *, expectation=None) at gaussian.py:240-282. The v2 version builds factor = sigma * identity(domain) and samples via the factor's domain.white_noise (gaussian.py:636), so it now produces the identity-covariance measure the v1 docstring promised rather than covariance G. For the probe role the randomised routines call `space.white_noise(rng=rng)` directly (spaces.py:292, 672-680; components ~ N(0, G^-1)). DESIGN.md section 9 documents the v1 version as a live bug and records the replacement; what was removed is the alias name, not the capability, and the capability is now correct. Caveat: the v2 measure only samples on spaces that implement white_noise -- MassWeightedSpace (spaces.py:802-950) does not, so from_standard_deviation(mass_weighted_space, 1.0).sample() raises NotImplementedError where v1's ran (see the random_range row). |
| `low_rank.LowRankSVD.sigma_factor` | Returns the diagonal operator Sigma of singular values on EuclideanSpace(k). | `LowRankSVD.singular_values (ndarray); DiagonalLinearOperator(EuclideanSpace(k), svd.singular_values) if an operator is needed` | No property returns Sigma as an operator. The values are exposed by `singular_values`; a user needing the diagonal operator writes `DiagonalLinearOperator(EuclideanSpace(svd.rank), svd.singular_values)` (pygeoinf2.algebra.diagonal:40-72, which accepts EuclideanSpace since it is an OrthonormalSpace(CoordinateSpace)). Grep 'sigma_factor' in pygeoinf2: no hits. |
| `low_rank.LowRankEig.d_factor` | Returns the diagonal operator D of eigenvalues on EuclideanSpace(k). | `LowRankEig.eigenvalues (ndarray); DiagonalLinearOperator(EuclideanSpace(k), eig.eigenvalues) if an operator is needed` | No property returns D as an operator; grep 'd_factor' in pygeoinf2: no hits. The values are `eigenvalues`; the operator form is `DiagonalLinearOperator(EuclideanSpace(eig.rank), eig.eigenvalues)` (algebra/diagonal.py:40-72). The is_galerkin flag on D has no v2 analogue (the coefficient space is Euclidean, so components and Galerkin coincide). |
| `low_rank.behaviour.geometric_safety_guard` | When no measure is supplied and the codomain's basis is not orthonormal (e.g. a mass-weighted or general HilbertSpace), random_range automatically constructs an N(0, I) white-noise measure on the domain and routes execution through the abstract, metric-aware Gram-Schmidt path so the returned Q is a true isometry in the codomain's inner product. | `random_range always orthonormalises in the codomain's own inner product (codomain.orthonormal_basis / _orthonormalise_columns with apply_gram) and probes with domain.white_noise` | There is no guard because there is no Euclidean-only path to guard against: both v2 paths (coordinate-free and component) use the codomain metric, and the probe distribution is identity-covariance on the space by construction (DESIGN §9 shows the v1 guard actually fed G-covariance probes). The returned basis is a true isometry in the codomain inner product on every space that implements white_noise (tests/test_randomised.py:42-50, and TestRandomisedOnADenseMetric at :381+). The v1 guard had a second job, though: by manufacturing a probe measure with white_noise_measure it made the routine RUN on every non-orthonormal v1 space. v2 runs only on spaces that provide white_noise -- CoordinateSpace (default: dense Gram Cholesky, spaces.py:364-381), DiagonalMetricSpace (:1015), ComponentView (:1101), OrthonormalSpace (:1132), DirectSum (direct_sum.py:214, 323), the MFEM backends (mfem_hilbert.py:265, 548); the generic MassWeightedSpace (spaces.py:802-950) does not and inherits the raising base method (:292-310), so the replacement covers fewer space classes than the guard did. What is also NOT reproducible: forcing the probe distribution to a user-supplied prior measure (v1 `measure=` override) -- see random_range row. grep 'is_orthonormal' in randomised.py: no hits. |

### nonlinear_optimisation — `nonlinear_optimisation.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nonlinear_optimisation.ScipyUnconstrainedOptimiser.minimize` | Minimises a NonLinearForm starting from x0 by converting to/from component arrays of form.domain and calling scipy.optimize.minimize with the stored method and options; returns the minimiser as a Vector of the domain. | `Optimiser.minimise(functional, x0, /) -> OptimisationResult, e.g. LBFGS(gtol=1e-8, max_iterations=500).minimise(phi, x0).minimiser` | Spelling minimize -> minimise; both arguments positional-only; `form: NonLinearForm` -> `functional: Functional`. Returns an OptimisationResult (minimiser, value, gradient_norm, iterations, evaluations, converged, message, history) instead of the bare Vector; the minimiser is result.minimiser. Works through space operations (copy, axpy, inner_product, norm) with no component round trip, so it runs on spaces without a coordinate map. Requires has_derivative (raises ValueError otherwise); NewtonCG/TrustRegionNewton additionally require has_hessian. Stopping adds rtol (relative to \|\|g0\|\|), ftol (relative value decrease) and a precision-loss outcome that v1/SciPy did not report. |
| `nonlinear_optimisation.ScipyUnconstrainedOptimiser.minimize.gradient_wrapper` | When the form has a gradient and the method is not derivative-free, SciPy receives the primal components of the Hilbert-space gradient (Riesz representative), not the dual components of the derivative. | `QuadraticModel.gradient = derivative.adjoint(1.0); slope = space.inner_product(gradient, direction) inside _DescentMethod/NewtonCG` | The v1 metric inconsistency (primal gradient components handed to SciPy as jac, which equals the Euclidean derivative only for G = I) no longer exists: the gradient is a domain vector obtained from the derivative through the adjoint (metric applied once, linearisation.py:74-83), and every slope is an inner product in the space (optimisation.py:246, :596). A user writes Functional.from_callables(domain, value, derivative=lambda x: LinearFunctional.from_derivative_components(domain, g)) and the optimiser does the rest. Tests exercise a non-diagonal Gram matrix (test_optimisation.py:628-644). |
| `nonlinear_optimisation.ScipyUnconstrainedOptimiser.minimize.hessian_wrapper` | For methods in _HESSIAN_METHODS and forms with has_hessian, the Hessian is supplied to SciPy as a matrix-free scipy LinearOperator built by LinearOperator.matrix(galerkin=True) (dense=False default), whose matvec maps components -> apply Hessian -> to_dual -> dual components. | `NewtonCG / TrustRegionNewton pass model.hessian (a LinearOperator) to truncated_cg, which only applies it` | Matrix-free is preserved and strengthened: the Hessian is consumed as an operator via hessian(direction) inside Steihaug CG (optimisation.py:785-840), with no SciPy LinearOperator and no Galerkin matrix. A user writes NewtonCG().minimise(phi, x0) or TrustRegionNewton().minimise(phi, x0) with phi built by Functional.from_callables(..., hessian=...) or gauss_newton_hessian (optimisation.py:856). Note for anyone hand-rolling a SciPy bridge: v2 LinearOperator.matrix(form='galerkin') is dense-only (operators.py:680-687) and no scipy.sparse.linalg.LinearOperator export exists (grep 'ScipyLinOp\|aslinearoperator\|as_scipy' over algebra/ and numerics/: no hits; the only sparse_linalg uses are splu/spilu in the preconditioner modules and backends/mfem.py's _to_scipy for MFEM matrices), so v1's dense=False Galerkin export has no v2 equivalent. |
| `nonlinear_optimisation.ScipyUnconstrainedOptimiser.minimize.result_handling` | The OptimizeResult is reduced to its `x` field and converted back to a domain Vector; success flag, message, iteration counts and final function value are not exposed and failure does not raise. | `OptimisationResult(minimiser, value, gradient_norm, iterations, evaluations, converged, message, history)` | IMPROVED: the v1 loss of convergence information is reversed. Every minimise returns converged and a message ('gradient tolerance reached', 'value tolerance reached', 'iteration limit reached', 'line search failed to find a suitable step', 'no further decrease is representable in double precision'), the final value, gradient norm, iteration and evaluation counts, and the value history. Failure still does not raise (matches v1); the caller inspects result.converged. |
| `nonlinear_optimisation.line_search.unbound_extra_condition_bug` | The final call passes `_extra_condition` unconditionally, but that local is only bound inside the `if extra_condition is not None` block, so calling line_search without an extra_condition raises UnboundLocalError. | `StrongWolfeLineSearch()(phi, x, p, value=f, slope=s) works unconditionally` | The v1 defect (UnboundLocalError whenever extra_condition was omitted, i.e. the function was unusable without a dummy predicate) cannot occur in v2 because there is no extra_condition parameter at all; the search is always callable. The intended spec (line search usable without an extra condition) is met, but by removing the feature rather than fixing the branch. |

### small_modules — `parallel.py, utils.py, auxiliary.py, config.py, datasets.py, dynamical_system.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `parallel.parallel_mat_mat` | Computes the product A @ B in parallel by applying A to each column of B in a separate joblib task and column-stacking the results into a dense ndarray. | `LinearOperator.apply_block(vectors, n_jobs=None) in pygeoinf2/algebra/operators.py:804-825, driven by parallel.parallel_map (pygeoinf2/parallel.py:139-182)` | The block product A @ B is now `operator.apply_block(list_of_vectors, n_jobs=k)` returning a list of codomain vectors (not a dense ndarray built from columns of B). Default is serial (n_jobs=None) where v1 defaulted to all cores (-1). Matrix-backed and diagonal operators override apply_block with one vectorised product (operators.py:1810-1826, diagonal.py:337) and expression nodes pass blocks through their parts (nodes.py:91,200,304,375,514,715). The randomised routines call it exactly where v1 called parallel_mat_mat (numerics/randomised.py:90,110,114,211,216,576,644,990). Review B verified apply_block(n_jobs=2) on a from_callables operator returns the right images under loky. |
| `parallel.parallel_compute_dense_matrix_from_scipy_op` | Forms the dense matrix of a scipy LinearOperator in parallel by applying it to every standard basis vector, one joblib task per column, and column-stacking. | `LinearOperator.matrix(form='auto', by='auto', n_jobs=None) in pygeoinf2/algebra/operators.py:680-770` | Dense-matrix formation with a parallel column loop is `operator.matrix(n_jobs=k)`; the per-column closure is handed to parallel_map (operators.py:737-746). Takes a pygeoinf2 LinearOperator, not a scipy LinearOperator (for a raw scipy op a user writes `parallel_map(lambda j: op @ np.eye(n)[j], range(n), n_jobs=k)`). Default serial, v1 defaulted to all cores. `_known_matrix` (operators.py:773-790) short-circuits probing for matrix-backed/composed operators. The row-fill route through the adjoint when codomain.dim < domain.dim is NOT new: v1 _compute_dense_matrix already returned adjoint.matrix(...).T / dual.matrix(...).T in that case (v1 linear_operators.py:832-847). What changed is that v1 guarded the row route with `not self.__using_default_dual_and_adjoint` (linear_operators.py:99-105, 834) and fell back to the column loop for an operator with no supplied adjoint, whereas v2 has no such guard: `by='auto'` (operators.py:725) picks rows purely on dimensions and the row closure calls self.adjoint (operators.py:753-770), which for a from_callables operator without an adjoint raises NotImplementedError (operators.py:1663-1669). REPRODUCED under the poetry venv: v2 `A = LinearOperator.from_callables(EuclideanSpace(5), EuclideanSpace(2), lambda x: M @ x); A.matrix()` raises NotImplementedError 'No adjoint action was supplied for this operator...'; `A.matrix(by='columns')` and `A.matrix(by='columns', n_jobs=2)` return M; v1 `inf.LinearOperator(X, Y, lambda x: M @ x).matrix(dense=True)` returns M. So the cited replacement of the v1 parallel function fails by default on a wide adjoint-less operator; the user must know to pass by='columns'. |
| `parallel._worker_compute_scipy_op_col` | Internal top-level worker that builds the j-th unit vector of length domain_dim and returns scipy_op @ e_j (one column of the dense matrix). | `the local `column(index)` closure inside LinearOperator.matrix, pygeoinf2/algebra/operators.py:739-746` | The per-column worker is a closure over the operator and `self.domain.basis_vector(index)`/`self.codomain.to_components`, passed to parallel_map; there is no top-level worker function. Picklability is obtained because closures over bound methods of ordinary objects pickle under loky (parallel.py:70-78). Unit vector is built by `domain.basis_vector(index)` rather than a raw float64 zeros array. |
| `auxiliary.empirical_data_error_measure` | Builds an empirical Gaussian data-error measure by pushing model_measure through forward_operator, drawing n_samples data-space samples, centring them on their sample mean, scaling by scale_factor, and calling GaussianMeasure.from_samples on the codomain. | `GaussianMeasure.from_samples (pygeoinf2/probability/gaussian.py:336-378) + ProbabilityMeasure.push_forward/__rmatmul__ (pygeoinf2/probability/base.py:293-326) + samples(n, rng=, n_jobs=) (base.py:76-115); scalar scaling via HilbertSpace.scale(a, x) (pygeoinf2/algebra/spaces.py:155), not multiply` | No helper function. The same measure is two lines: `draws = (B @ prior).samples(10, rng=rng); mu = GaussianMeasure.from_samples(B.codomain, [B.codomain.scale(scale_factor, d) for d in draws])`. Note the method name: v1 auxiliary.py:26-27 used `data_space.multiply(a, x)` for scalar scaling; in v2 `multiply(x, y)` is the abstract HilbertModule pointwise product (spaces.py:758, only on module spaces), so scalar scaling must be `space.scale(a, x)` (spaces.py:155). from_samples already subtracts the sample mean (gaussian.py:360-361) so v1's manual centring is redundant; scaling the draws by scale_factor scales the covariance by scale_factor**2 as v1 did. Differences: v1 result mean is the (zero) sample mean of centred samples; v2 from_samples mean is the sample mean of the scaled draws (nonzero) unless the user centres first. from_samples needs >= 2 samples (gaussian.py:356-358) where v1 GaussianMeasure.from_samples accepted n=1 with a zero covariance (v1 gaussian_measure.py:304-308); takes an explicit rng. The 1/(n-1) normalisation (gaussian.py:362) is unchanged from v1 (gaussian_measure.py:314,320). The construction is exercised by tests/test_probability.py:241-256. |
| `config.DATADIR` | Absolute path of the package's bundled data directory (pygeoinf/data), shipped inside the wheel and treated as read-only; holds the seed datasets gsn_stations.csv and usgs_event_cache.csv. | `the package `pygeoinf2.data` (pygeoinf2/data/__init__.py:1), read via importlib.resources.files('pygeoinf2.data') in pygeoinf2/symmetric_space/sphere.py:1954-1959` | No DATADIR constant and no pygeoinf2 config module (grep 'DATADIR' over pygeoinf2/**/*.py: none). The data directory is a real subpackage; a user wanting the path writes `from importlib.resources import files; files('pygeoinf2.data')`. CSVs are included in the wheel via pyproject.toml:44. Still read-only in practice: nothing writes there. |

### gaussian_measure — `gaussian_measure.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gaussian_measure.GaussianMeasure.inverse_covariance_set` | True if an inverse covariance (precision) operator is stored. | `measure.precision is not None` | No boolean property; write `measure.precision is not None`. Also has_log_density / has_grad_log_density are True exactly when a precision is present. |
| `gaussian_measure.GaussianMeasure.covariance_factor_set` | True if a covariance factor L with C = L @ L* is stored. | `measure.covariance_factor is not None` | No boolean property; test the property against None. |
| `gaussian_measure.GaussianMeasure.inverse_covariance_factor_set` | True if an inverse covariance factor Li with C^-1 = Li* @ Li is stored. | `measure.precision_factor is not None` | No boolean property. |
| `gaussian_measure.GaussianMeasure.deflated_pointwise_std` | Pointwise standard deviation = domain.vector_sqrt of deflated_pointwise_variance with the same arguments. | `np.sqrt(space.pointwise_variance_at(measure, points, rank=r, samples=s))` | No std wrapper; take np.sqrt of the ndarray returned by pointwise_variance_at (SymmetricSpace only). |
| `gaussian_measure.GaussianMeasure.directional_statistics` | Returns (expectation, variance) of the scalar Gaussian <x, direction>: (<m, d>, <C d, d>). | `(domain.inner_product(mu.expectation, d), mu.directional_variance(d))` | No tuple-returning method. grep 'directional_statistics' in pygeoinf2 -> only a test name (tests/test_spectral.py:329) that calls directional_variance/directional_covariance. review/r2_probability_inference.md:26 records it as absent. |
| `gaussian_measure.GaussianMeasure.zero_expectation` | Returns a copy of the measure with the same covariance and zero expectation. | `mu.translate(mu.domain.negative(mu.expectation))` | No method; translate goes through _combine_affine with the identity, keeping factor, covariance, precision and precision_factor (better than v1, which dropped the precision). For an explicit-sampler measure without a factor the result IS correctly centred: the closure returns identity(s + m) + (-m) = s, the stored expectation is the zero vector, and sample() adds that zero (verified: sample mean ~0 for a hand-built sampler measure and for a condition() result). The double-mean bug bites only when the new mean is non-zero. One real difference from v1: the result's has_zero_expectation is False (a zero vector is stored, not the None sentinel), whereas v1 zero_expectation stored None. |
| `gaussian_measure.GaussianMeasure.__neg__` | Returns the measure with negated expectation and the same covariance. | `-1.0 * mu (ProbabilityMeasure.__mul__ / __rmul__ -> GaussianMeasure._combine_scale)` | Unary minus is NOT defined: `-mu` raises TypeError (verified: "bad operand type for unary -: 'GaussianMeasure'"). Use -1.0 * mu, which negates the expectation, keeps the covariance (alpha^2 = 1), negates the factor, and keeps precision/precision_factor (v1 dropped the precision). Unlike v1 __neg__, which wrapped an explicit sampler as -sample(), -1.0 * mu drops the explicit sampler (verified (-1*mu).can_sample False for an explicit-sampler, factor-less measure) and stores a vector mean (has_zero_expectation False for a centred input). |

### convex_analysis — `convex_analysis.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `convex_analysis.SupportFunction._subgradient_impl` | The callback registered with NonLinearForm as the form's subgradient; delegates to support_point(q) and raises NotImplementedError('Support point not available; subgradient cannot be computed.') when that returns None. | `SupportFunction.subgradient(y) calls self._maximiser(y) directly (numerics/convex.py:262-264)` | No separate registered callback: subgradient() itself delegates to _maximiser(). The None -> NotImplementedError('Support point not available...') translation is gone, so a missing maximiser yields None silently (oracle/shifted supports) rather than an exception. has_subgradient is hard-coded True exactly as in v1, with the same 'claims available, fails at call time' defect. |
| `convex_analysis.SupportFunction.translate` | Return the support function of the translated set C + p, h(q) = h_C(q) + <q, p>. | `h + SupportFunction.of_point(h.domain, p)  (functional level); ConvexSet.translate(vector) -> _Translated whose support_function() is _ShiftedSupport (set level; Ball/Ellipsoid.translate return a new Ball/Ellipsoid instead)` | No translate on SupportFunction. The functional-level route via + of_point yields a _MinkowskiSupport whose maximiser propagates (x*(q) + p), matching v1. The set-level _ShiftedSupport computes only the value (h_K(y) + <v, y>) and defines no _maximiser, so its subgradient silently returns None — a regression against v1 translate, whose result carried the support point. _Translated also inherits the raising ConvexSet.support_maximiser. |
| `convex_analysis.SupportFunction.scale` | Return the support function of the scaled set alpha*C, h(q) = alpha*h_C(q), for alpha >= 0. | `alpha * h  or  h * alpha  (SupportFunction.__mul__), for Python int/float alpha > 0 -> _ScaledSupport; also h / alpha via Operator.__truediv__` | No scale method. Only alpha > 0 of type int/float (np.float64 passes, being a float subclass) stays a SupportFunction; alpha == 0 or numpy scalar types on the right (h * np.int64(2), h * np.float32(2)) fall back to a generic _FunctionalScaled (not a SupportFunction, and its subgradient raises). On the left, np.int64(2) * h does give _ScaledSupport because numpy scalar arithmetic unboxes to a Python int before calling h.__rmul__, so the result depends on operand order. v1's alpha >= 0 with ValueError for alpha < 0 is replaced by silently accepting negatives as generic functionals. h / alpha (alpha > 0) is new and yields _ScaledSupport. |
| `convex_analysis.HalfSpaceSupportFunction.normal_vector` | The half-space normal vector a. | `geometry.convex.HalfSpace(domain, normal, /, *, offset=0.0).normal` | The normal is a property of the v2 HalfSpace set (renamed normal_vector -> normal, constructor argument positional-only). There is no support-function object to carry it. |
| `convex_analysis.HalfSpaceSupportFunction.offset` | The half-space offset b. | `geometry.convex.HalfSpace(...).offset` | Same name and meaning, but on the set; keyword-only constructor argument with default 0.0 (v1 required it). |
| `convex_analysis.HalfSpaceSupportFunction.inequality_type` | The convention string, '<=' or '>='. | `HalfSpace(domain, domain.scale(-1.0, a), offset=-b) for the '>=' convention; only '<=' is representable directly` | v2 HalfSpace models only {x : (normal, x) <= offset}; the '>=' convention is obtained by negating normal and offset. There is no property recording the convention (grep 'inequality_type' in pygeoinf2: none). |

### convex_optimisation — `convex_optimisation.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `convex_optimisation.SubgradientDescent.oracle` | Returns the NonLinearForm objective supplied at construction. | `the Functional the caller passes to SubgradientDescent.minimise(functional, x0)` | The optimiser no longer holds the objective, so there is no property; the user already holds the functional they pass to minimise(). |
| `convex_optimisation.SubgradientDescent.domain` | Returns oracle.domain, the Hilbert space of the decision variable. | `functional.domain` | No property on the optimiser; read functional.domain on the Functional passed to minimise(). |
| `convex_optimisation.Cut` | Dataclass recording one linearisation of a convex function: evaluation point x, value f, subgradient g, and the iteration index at which it was generated; defines the affine lower bound f + <g, lambda - x>. | `(gradient, value, point) tuples in ProximalBundleMethod.minimise / LevelBundleMethod.minimise` | No class. Each cut is a plain tuple (subgradient, f, x) appended to a local list; the iteration index is not recorded. |
| `convex_optimisation.Bundle` | Ordered collection of Cut objects with helpers to build the piecewise-linear cutting-plane model hat_phi(lambda)=max_j[f_j+<g_j,lambda-x_j>] for proximal and level bundle methods. | `local list `cuts` inside ProximalBundleMethod.minimise / LevelBundleMethod.minimise` | No Bundle class; a Python list of (gradient, value, point) tuples local to each minimise() call. Not user-constructible or inspectable. |
| `convex_optimisation.Bundle.add_cut` | Appends a Cut to the bundle. | `cuts.append((space.copy(slope(x)), value, space.copy(x)))` | list.append on the local cuts list; v2 copies the subgradient and point vectors (v1 stored references). |
| `convex_optimisation.Bundle.__len__` | Number of cuts currently stored. | `len(cuts)` | Plain len() on the local list, used only for the capacity check. |
| `convex_optimisation.Bundle.compress` | Discards all but the max_size most recent cuts (FIFO truncation). | ``if len(cuts) > self._capacity: cuts.pop(0)` in both minimise loops` | Same FIFO drop-oldest rule, keyed on the `capacity` constructor argument (v1 bundle_size). Default capacity 40 for ProximalBundleMethod (v1 100), 100 for LevelBundleMethod (same). |

### subsets — `subsets.py`

| v1 | what it did | v2 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `subsets.Ellipsoid.radius` | The radius parameter r (level is r**2). | `Ellipsoid(X, (1.0 / r**2) * A, centre=c, covariance=r**2 * A_inv)` | No radius parameter or property; v2 ellipsoids are always at level 1, so a radius-r ellipsoid is built by scaling the precision by 1/r^2 (and the covariance by r^2). Positive scalar scaling preserves SELF_ADJOINT\|POSITIVE_DEFINITE (traits.py:114-116; inference/backus.py:485-492 uses this pattern), so the recipe passes the trait check for r > 0. The subsumption is PARTIAL: v1 accepted radius 0 (subsets.py:908-909 rejects only negatives, giving the degenerate set {c}); 1/r**2 is a ZeroDivisionError and v2 has no way to express an infinite precision. Only Ball keeps the radius-0 case. |
| `subsets.Ellipsoid.normalized` | Returns the same set expressed with radius 1 by scaling the operator by 1/r^2. | `Every v2 Ellipsoid is already normalised (level 1)` | No normalized property; nothing to normalise because radius is folded into the precision at construction. |
| `subsets.NormalisedEllipsoid` | Ellipsoid with radius fixed to 1: {x \| <A(x-c), x-c> <= 1}. | `Ellipsoid(X, A, centre=c)` | v2 Ellipsoid is always the radius-1 set {<P(x-c),x-c> <= 1}; NormalisedEllipsoid is therefore the plain constructor. (Unlike v1's NormalisedEllipsoid it can take covariance= and so has a support function.) |
| `subsets.EllipsoidSurface.radius` | The radius parameter r. | `EllipsoidSurface(X, (1.0 / r**2) * A, centre=c)` | No radius; scale the precision. As for Ellipsoid.radius, r = 0 is not expressible (v1 accepted it). |
| `subsets.EllipsoidSurface.normalized` | Returns EllipsoidSurface(domain, center, 1.0, operator / r^2). | `Always normalised` | Level is fixed at 1 so there is nothing to normalise. |
| `subsets.HyperPlane.normal_norm` | \|\|a\|\| computed via domain.norm on each access (not cached). | `X.norm(hyperplane.normal)` | No public property; the squared norm is cached privately in _squared_norm (convex.py:699) and used by project. |
| `subsets.HyperPlane.distance_to` | Perpendicular distance \|<a,x> - b\| / \|\|a\|\|. | `X.norm(X.subtract(x, hyperplane.project(x)))` | No distance_to method (grep 'distance_to\\|signed_distance' over pygeoinf2 -> none); the perpendicular distance is the norm of x minus its projection, at the cost of a vector op rather than one inner product. |

No property records which form was intended. |
